title: Decision 33 COM 7A.26: Deletion of the Dresden Elbe Valley from the World Heritage List (2009), and the preceding Danger List decisions (2006-2008)
body: UNESCO World Heritage Committee (33rd session, Seville, 2009; this is a decision of the World Heritage Committee, not a court or UN Security Council action)
case_reference: Decisions 33 COM 7A.26 and 33 COM 8C.3 (preceded by 30 COM 7B.77, 31 COM 7A.27 and 32 COM 7A.26)
summary: The Dresden Elbe Valley, Germany, was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2004. In 2006 the World Heritage Committee (30th session, Vilnius), in Decision 30 COM 7B.77, found that the planned Waldschlösschen Bridge, a four-lane crossing inside the property's core zone, 'would irreversibly damage the values and integrity of the property', asked for the project to be halted and inscribed the property on the List of World Heritage in Danger. The City of Dresden told UNESCO that the project followed a citizens' referendum; a court in Bautzen concluded, in a decision the World Heritage Centre received on 13 March 2007, that the public vote had to be implemented. The Committee kept the property on the Danger List in 2007 (31 COM 7A.27) and 2008 (32 COM 7A.26), warning in 2007 that it would be deleted if bridge construction had an irreversible impact on the property's Outstanding Universal Value, and in 2008 that deletion would follow in 2009 if works continued and the damage was not reversed. Construction began in August 2007. On 25 June 2009 at its 33rd session in Seville the Committee, in Decision 33 COM 7A.26, decided to delete the property from the World Heritage List and, in Decision 33 COM 8C.3, removed it from the Danger List. UNESCO describes it as the second property ever deleted from the List. The German Foreign Office said it regretted the decision.
legal_basis: The World Heritage Convention (1972) is the treaty read for this entry. Article 4 says the duty of ensuring the protection and conservation of the heritage on its territory 'belongs primarily to that State'. Article 6(1) says the States Parties recognise that such heritage is a world heritage 'for whose protection it is the duty of the international community as a whole to co-operate'. Article 11(4) provides for a list of World Heritage in Danger, which may include only property 'threatened by serious and specific dangers'; Article 11(5) says the Committee defines the criteria for inclusion in either list. The Danger List decisions were taken under these provisions as applied by the Committee. The Convention articles read contain no provision on deleting a property from the World Heritage List; the Committee's decisions cite the Operational Guidelines (Decision 30 COM 7B.77 cites paragraph 179(b) of the Operational Guidelines for its finding of irreversible damage, 31 COM 7A.27 cites paragraphs 192-198 of the Operational Guidelines for its decision to delete the property if the bridge had an irreversible impact, and 33 COM 7A.26 refers to Section III of the Operational Guidelines for a new nomination). The text of the Operational Guidelines was not read for this entry, so the Guidelines' wording on deletion is not stated here. Decision 33 COM 7A.26 recalls Article 6(1) and the State Party's obligation to protect and conserve the heritage on its territory, and notes 'with deep regret' that the State Party could not fulfil its Convention obligations.
outcome: (1) Decision 30 COM 7B.77 (30th session, Vilnius, 2006): found that the bridge would irreversibly damage the values and integrity of the property, requested the State Party and City authorities to urgently halt the project, and decided to inscribe the property on the List of World Heritage in Danger, with a view to considering delisting at the 31st session in 2007 'if the plans are carried out'. (2) Decision 31 COM 7A.27 (31st session, Christchurch, 2007): asked the State Party to continue its efforts to find a solution, applied reinforced monitoring, retained the property on the Danger List, and decided to delete it if bridge construction had an irreversible impact on its Outstanding Universal Value. (3) Decision 32 COM 7A.26 (32nd session, Quebec City, 2008): regretted that construction had proceeded, strongly requested an immediate halt and urged reconsideration of the tunnel option, retained the property on the Danger List, and warned of deletion in 2009 if works continued and the damage was not reversed. (4) Decision 33 COM 7A.26 (33rd session, Seville, 2009): 'Decides to delete the Dresden Elbe Valley (Germany) from the World Heritage List'; it regretted that the Committee's requests had failed to protect the property and that the project had not been halted and the damage not reversed, noted the State Party's commitment to explore options to preserve the Outstanding Universal Value, and considered that a new nomination for Dresden's heritage could be envisaged under Section III of the Operational Guidelines. (5) Decision 33 COM 8C.3 (same session): removed the Dresden Elbe Valley from the List of World Heritage in Danger. The sources read do not state whether the 2009 decisions were taken by vote or consensus, and do not state the days on which the 2006-2008 decisions were adopted.
interpretation: These are statements by named bodies and authors, not findings of this entry. The German Federal Foreign Office (Minister of State Günter Gloser, 25 June 2009) said it regretted the Committee's decision, that despite intensive efforts no compromise had been reached, and that 'Dresden ist ein Einzelfall' (Dresden is an isolated case) (src_11). UNESCO's news item of 25 June 2009 says the property failed to keep its 'outstanding universal value as inscribed', quotes the session chair, María Jesús San Segundo, as saying 'Every time we fail to preserve a site, we share the pain of the State Party', and says any new nomination would have to be presented under different criteria and boundaries (src_09). UNESCO's news item of 4 July 2008 says the Committee gave Dresden more time because of legal proceedings in Germany (src_05). Sabine von Schorlemer, professor of international law at TU Dresden, titled her 2009 article 'Blamage für Deutschland' (a disgrace for Germany); she writes that the federal government kept a restrained stance, argues that voters in the 2005 referendum were not given key information about the bridge's effect on World Heritage status, and cites Federal Transport Minister Wolfgang Tiefensee, as reported in the Süddeutsche Zeitung of 26 June 2009, as saying 'Welterbestätten sind nationale Aufgaben' (World Heritage sites are national responsibilities) (src_12). Douglas Schoch's article abstract says that courts and local polls supported the bridge while critics 'denounced' it as an eyesore and an affront to the ideals of World Heritage (src_13). Only the abstract of Schoch was read.
start_date_display: 2006 (30th session, Vilnius; the adoption day is not stated in the sources read)
end_date_display: 2009-06-25 (UNESCO news item dated 25 June 2009; the decision pages give the year only)

timeline.title: Dresden Elbe Valley inscribed on the World Heritage List
timeline.description: UNESCO's 2009 news item states the property was inscribed in 2004. Decision 30 COM 7B.77 recalls the 2004 inscription as a cultural landscape.

timeline.title: Dresden citizens' referendum on the Waldschlösschen Bridge
timeline.description: Sabine von Schorlemer (src_12) refers to the 2005 Dresden citizens' referendum on the bridge, with a binding force of three years; she gives no vote count. UNESCO's 2006 report records the City of Dresden's statement that the bridge project followed an international architectural competition and 'a referendum of the citizens of Dresden' that approved it. The UNESCO documents read give no date or result for the vote.

timeline.title: ICOMOS comments on the planned bridge
timeline.description: UNESCO's 2006 report records that on 10 January 2006 ICOMOS said the crossing was 'no longer an urban bridge' and would considerably disturb the property, and called for a pause and for alternatives including a tunnel. The report also records an independent visual impact study by RWTH Aachen, received by the World Heritage Centre in April 2006, and the City of Dresden's statement that traffic assessments showed a need for an additional river crossing.

timeline.title: 30th session (Vilnius): Decision 30 COM 7B.77 inscribes the property on the Danger List
timeline.description: The Committee found, citing paragraph 179(b) of the Operational Guidelines, that the bridge 'would irreversibly damage the values and integrity of the property'. It 'Requests the State Party and the City authorities to urgently halt this construction project' and 'Decides to inscribe the property on the List of World Heritage in Danger', with a view to considering delisting at its 31st session in 2007 'if the plans are carried out'. The adopted decision notes that the City had suspended the project until the session.

timeline.title: World Heritage Centre receives the decision of the Bautzen court
timeline.description: UNESCO's 2007 report states that on 13 March 2007 the Centre 'received the decision of the court case in Bautzen (Sächsisches Oberverwaltungsgericht)' in a case between the City of Dresden and the Land Sachsen, and that the court concluded that 'the public vote for the construction of the bridge has to be implemented'. The report records that the Land Sachsen had requested that the procedure continue in accordance with the public vote and that the City Council had halted the project. The date is when the Centre received the decision; the court's judgment itself was not read and the report gives no ruling date.

timeline.title: 31st session (Christchurch): Decision 31 COM 7A.27 keeps the property on the Danger List
timeline.description: The Committee noted that the City Council had halted the project and a court case between the City and the Land had followed; taking into account that the judicial process had been exhausted, it asked the State Party to 'continue its efforts to find an appropriate solution' and submit alternatives by 1 October 2007, applied the reinforced monitoring mechanism, retained the property on the Danger List, and decided to delete it from the World Heritage List (citing paragraphs 192-198 of the Operational Guidelines) if bridge construction had an irreversible impact on its Outstanding Universal Value.

timeline.title: Construction of the bridge begins
timeline.description: UNESCO's 2009 state of conservation page lists August 2007 as the start of construction of the Waldschlösschen Bridge.

timeline.title: Reinforced monitoring mission
timeline.description: A World Heritage Centre/ICOMOS reinforced monitoring mission visited the property while foundation excavation was under way. UNESCO's 2008 report records its conclusion that the chosen Elbe crossing would have a considerable, irreversible negative impact on the property's Outstanding Universal Value, that a tunnel would likely have a much smaller impact, and that a redesigned bridge would likely have a comparable negative impact.

timeline.title: 32nd session (Quebec City): Decision 32 COM 7A.26
timeline.description: The Committee regretted that construction had been allowed to proceed, 'Strongly requests the State Party to immediately halt the current construction works', urged reconsideration of the tunnel option, decided to continue to apply the Reinforced Monitoring mechanism, requested a report by 1 February 2009, and retained the property on the Danger List, with deletion at the 33rd session in 2009 'if the planned works on the bridge continue and the damage already caused is not reversed'. UNESCO's news item of 4 July 2008 says the Committee gave Dresden more time because of legal proceedings in Germany.

timeline.title: Germany's update report
timeline.description: UNESCO's 2009 page summarises an update report from the Permanent Delegation of Germany dated 28 January 2009: it states that 'all legal procedures at Courts' concerning halting or changing the project were completed and that 'the bridge is being built as planned'. The Advisory Bodies and the World Heritage Centre assessed that the requests to halt had not been addressed and that the infrastructure works had 'impacted irreversibly on the integrity and outstanding universal value of the property'.

timeline.title: 33rd session (Seville): Decision 33 COM 7A.26 deletes the property; Decision 33 COM 8C.3 removes it from the Danger List
timeline.description: The Committee decided to delete the Dresden Elbe Valley (Germany) from the World Heritage List. In the same session, Decision 33 COM 8C.3 decided to remove it from the List of World Heritage in Danger. UNESCO's news item of 25 June 2009 describes it as the second property ever removed from the List, after Oman's Arabian Oryx Sanctuary in 2007.

timeline.title: German Federal Foreign Office statement
timeline.description: Minister of State Günter Gloser stated that he regretted the Committee's decision ('Ich bedaure die Entscheidung des Welterbekomitees') and that, despite intensive efforts, no compromise had been reached.

changelog.change: Initial draft. Premise checked and confirmed: 33rd session, Seville; deletion decision is 33 COM 7A.26 and the Danger List removal is 33 COM 8C.3 (both confirmed on UNESCO's decision pages); preceding decisions 30 COM 7B.77 (Vilnius 2006), 31 COM 7A.27 (Christchurch 2007), 32 COM 7A.26 (Quebec City 2008). case_type OTHER: the World Heritage Committee is an intergovernmental treaty body, not a court or tribunal (so not INTERNATIONAL_COURT or TRIBUNAL) and not a Security Council or UN General Assembly action; the Odesa entry uses the same value. Correction to the existing site dossier: it says a court 'ruled' on 13 March 2007; UNESCO's report says the Centre RECEIVED the Bautzen court decision on that date, so this entry uses that wording. Known gaps: (1) whc.unesco.org could not be fetched directly (proxy refused the host); all UNESCO pages were read through a summarising fetch tool with a short-quote limit, so decision wording is quoted only where the tool returned it verbatim and full decision texts were not independently re-read; the Convention articles were read the same way. (2) Operational Guidelines text (paragraph 179(b), deletion paragraphs, Section III) not read; no paragraph is quoted. (3) The referendum: only the year 2005 (von Schorlemer) and the City of Dresden's statement as recorded by UNESCO; no date, turnout or result found in a primary source. (4) German court proceedings are known only through UNESCO's report of the Bautzen (Sächsisches Oberverwaltungsgericht) decision; the judgment, other court rulings and any Federal Constitutional Court involvement were not found or read. (5) Adoption days of the 2006-2008 decisions and the 2009 decision are not on the pages; 25 June 2009 comes from UNESCO's news item; whether decisions were by vote or consensus is not stated. (6) The Committee's session report and the Operational Guidelines were not opened; Germany's own January 2009 report is read only as summarised by UNESCO. (7) Schoch (2014) is abstract-only. (8) The 2006 Danger List decision 30 COM 8C.1 and the 31st session news item were not opened. (9) Bundestag committee material and the Saxon government's position were not found in sources opened for this entry.

Independent verification against UNESCO decision pages and SOC reports (30 COM 7B.77, 31 COM 7A.27, 32 COM 7A.26, 33 COM 7A.26, 33 COM 8C.3 numbers, sessions, cities and 25 June 2009 date all confirmed), news items 447 and 522, Convention text, Auswaertiges Amt release (Gloser: 'Ich bedaure...', 'Dresden ist ein Einzelfall', no compromise), von Schorlemer (restrained federal stance, Tiefensee/SZ 26 June 2009) and Schoch abstract. Fixes: (1) 2006 decision now carries the Committee's condition 'if the plans are carried out' (summary/outcome/timeline); (2) summary no longer blends 2007 and 2008 deletion wording; (3) 31 COM 7A.27 timeline wording aligned to the text ('judicial process has been exhausted', paragraphs 192-198 cited) and legal_basis notes this citation; (4) 32 COM reinforced-monitoring wording aligned to the text; (5) removed unsupported 'many' before critics in the Schoch abstract summary. Not verified: Operational Guidelines text; the Bautzen judgment; vote vs consensus; full Convention/decision texts were read through a summarising tool. German positions are attributed to the Foreign Office/Minister Gloser and, for Tiefensee, as reported by von Schorlemer citing the SZ (not read directly).
